utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we resume the examination-in-chief of Mr. Sabljica, we have a few items to deal with first. I'd like to start first with the minor ones. I think there are two. The Prosecution committed itself to giving further information in respect of documents and tangible objects such as shrapnel pieces, whether they could be located, orders, maps. Mr. Ierace, could you inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have nothing further to add on the topic of shrapnel, although I should add that the Defence was informed last year, towards the end of last year, of what artifacts, if I could use that word, generally were in our possession and available for inspection. But as to shrapnel relating to the Markale market incident, I have nothing further to add. In relation to maps, in fact, I think that is the issue raised by the Prosecution of orders, maps as a topic arose in that context. Yesterday, I filed with the Registry a response in that regard. Do you have that, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't seen anything that has been filed yesterday, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I may have some copies here, Mr. President, which I'll hand up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, did you receive already a copy or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we talking about a letter dated the 5th? Because we received yesterday, Mr. Ierace -- are we talking here about a letter which is dated the 5th but which we received yesterday? Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace is trying to sort out things as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to insist on this. We did receive a document which is dated the 5th, but we received it yesterday, sometime during yesterday. It's a document -- no, it was the 11th. It was the 11th. We received it yesterday. It's two pages long. I don't know if that's the document that Mr. Ierace is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President. I could provide copies within five minutes, or I could just shortly summarise what that document contains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since both parties know what is in the documents, is there any need to discuss them at this very moment. If yes, I'd like to have copies. If no, then we'll see the copies sometime during this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since you yourself raised the question about the information of the shrapnel and the maps and orders, we've got to talk about it. Because you yourself raised that issue. There is an initial answer from the response, but it isn't a definitive answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that this is not a satisfactory answer to the Defence, and they would like to discuss it. Then, please, could you provide us with copies, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My case manager will provide copies in the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps then meanwhile, we continue with the other issues still.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the 92 bis issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but before going to that, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we still had an issue of yesterday which I'd like not to discuss in the presence of the witness. You objected against a leading question about the shelling investigated by the witness on Dobrinja. And it was a bit different from what we usually do in this courtroom, and I invited you to explain why this leading question was, in your view, inadmissible but not do it in the presence of the witness. So if you could give us any further information about that. We talked about disputed areas and areas not in dispute, and I had some difficulties yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't quite remember the specific passages. I think that we're talking about an issue of formulation. We could go back into the transcript and see exactly why. But the idea was as follows: I believe that we started from the principal that each time there were casualties, and we know as you have just said of among at least one of the three shellings that was mentioned in the chart that was supplied by the witness, there were no casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I don't think it was about that. When the -- when Mr. Stamp yesterday moved from the shelling on the 5th of February to the shelling of the 4th of February, part of his question was whether the witness investigated a shelling on the 4th of February in Dobrinja. And you objected against Dobrinja being part of the question and causing the question to be leading. And the answer of Mr. Stamp was that he was not aware that the fact that this shelling on the 4th of February in Dobrinja was in dispute. And since I'd rather not discuss whether something is in dispute or not in the presence of the witness, I gave you the opportunity to explain to us later why this certainly leading element of the question was not acceptable to the Defence where many, many other elements in question being just as leading were acceptable. So it was just for the better of the understanding of the Chamber that I'd like to give you the opportunity to explain why this element was unacceptable. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I go back to what I said. I've got to look exactly at what was said yesterday. I'll go back into the transcript if the Chamber gives me the opportunity to do so. But what was not acceptable was to ask a question in a very general way about several incidents saying that there were casualties when some of the incidents did not cause any casualties. That is the thing which I found to be leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was asking you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the Defence does not contest the fact that the shelling actually took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was asking you a question about another objection, as a matter of fact. But please look it up in the transcript, and whenever you have an answer to Dobrinja being a part of the -- being the leading element in the question, inform the Court. If you'd just give us two or three minutes so that we can read the answer of Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite the Defence to give whatever comment they would like to make at this moment or whatever observations they would like to make in respect of the response, the written response, by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I'll be pleased to do so. Thank you for giving me the time to try to confer with my colleagues, because we did not receive a translation of the letter dated the 11th, whereas we know how important that is for the Defence. Therefore, General Galic sitting behind me was not even available to become familiar with the contents of the documents which we received in our mail box this morning apparently. Mr. President, there are two points: The mechanical elements which we call shrapnel and the documentary elements which are the orders and maps as regards to point A, which relates to the shrapnel, I note that we asked on several occasions that the Prosecutor tell us how and when it was able to get those -- that information. I did not single line, not a single word in point A which refers specifically to those interventions or, as the case might be, to the shrapnel itself. Stated otherwise, the most essential elements for the Defence on which we could base ourselves in order to determine what actually happened during that incident in the Markale market, that information, through some kind of magic which I cannot explain, has vanished. We know that the information exists. We know that there are about 100 pieces of information but those elements have completely vanished. And I must say, Mr. President, and say it clearly that I increasingly have the impression that they do not want that information to be delivered to us and be subject to an evaluation. I simply point out that the Prosecution is not in the position to provide these elements which are vital for the Defence, and each person here must take into account the fact that for us the most important information or facts ascribed to his Excellency, General Galic, not one of the documents could be found which the Defence could then produce for the Chamber. My personal conclusion is that I-- and I have no doubt that that will be the same conclusion that the Chamber will come to also. The second point, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we deal with the items separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, what does the Prosecution intend to do in order to see whether the shrapnel pieces can be traced or what has been done in order to come to your final conclusion that they cannot be located? I mean, what efforts are made, what efforts still will be made, to see whether they can be located and perhaps transferred to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's a subject of -- it has been a subject of inquiries of the relevant authorities in Sarajevo. Certainly the impression I have is that there are no further inquiries that we could profitably make to obtain them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us when for the last time did you inquire of the local authorities on whether they could be found? I heard there was a movement of buildings and they might be lost during the removal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I could do that. I couldn't do that today. But if you wish me to report on that, then I certainly will. It would take me approximately one week to make those inquiries. The relevant investigator is not in The Hague at the moment. I would like to speak to him before I responded to the Trial Chamber. So perhaps next week I could inform the Trial Chamber of what steps have been taken to recover those pieces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Ierace, please inform the Chamber in due time. You said it would be approximately a week, on what exactly has been done and what's the latest information and the latest steps you've taken in order to obtain them. At the same time, I address the Defence that -- the Defence, of course, is entitled as well to try to get hold of these pieces. And as you know, in the system we are using in this Court, it's not like in many civil law systems, that the other party is responsible for the investigations and for the -- well, seeking the material to support its own case. So I'd very much like the Defence also to take whatever necessary steps and inform the Chamber if they fail to achieve a positive result to inform the Chamber on what the Defence has done and whether the Defence needs in whatever way in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence the assistance of the Court. So please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, proceed on the second item which is not the artifacts any more, but the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving me the floor again, Mr. President. Short comment for the transcript, on page 6, line 16, I was referring to the English transcript, I mentioned his Excellency General Galic and it didn't come up that way in the text. I don't want there to be any mistakes there. The other point, and I thank you for your concern in respect of the Defence, the Defence will do, I should say, everything it can, it will bend over backwards to find these documents, but your Chamber must be aware of the fact General Galic's counsel are not welcome at the MUP, and I don't think that we will find much cooperation from the Sarajevo authorities. But I will write to them personally, according to your suggestion, and we will see what kind of answer I get. Having said this, as regards to point B, that is, the documents: Mr. President, I note one thing, that in fact that there were documents in the possession of the Prosecution. This is the result of this two-page letter dated 11 March, 2002, and the Defence now discovers almost right now we are being told that those documents will not be disclosed to the Defence because they allegedly do not deal with the Sarajevo events in a more or less direct way or even an indirect way. This is the only reason, apparently, why the documents whose existence cannot be questioned today would not be disclosed. And one must indicate, Mr. President, that that is to disregard completely unfortunately the structure of a modern army. What we are asking is that we receive documents from the organisation which is at the very top of the command Hierarchy and pyramid. That general staff, that's what it's called, gave instructions to various armies including the first army. These armies can move around. Weapons can move around. Human and material resources can move around. And therefore, what is very important for the Defence to be able to determine and to understand is how the troops moved around as well as the weapons and how the orders were given in respect of this. The reason for this is a simple one. As the Prosecution blames the General for having participated in a campaign -- not the campaign itself but of setting up the campaign. Therefore, Mr. President, at some point we were able to demonstrate that there was a combat. We could demonstrate that the combat was significant, and that it took place on certain dates close to or sometimes the same dates as those of the incidents which are mentioned. What we are saying is the following: Among other things, during the combat phase, there were transports of men and troops and resources. We can show this thanks to the documents which are today in the possession of the Prosecution and which deal with the entire -- and I repeat -- the entire organisation at the top of the army. And without being able to demonstrate what we have already indicated, we will find ourselves in great difficulty in order to do what we must do properly, that is, do our best for the defence of General Galic. Therefore, in order to divide this all up into different areas as if the army was blind in respect of the territorial departments it was composed of, and in some ways, this is an illusion and imagined. There was not that system of compartmentalisation in this organisation or in any military organisation. These are frequently interconnected and we absolutely must in light of the chain of command be in a position to have that information. Therefore, Mr. President, as regards both these elements, that is, those having to do with physical objects like the shells, the shrapnel, and the documents, which have been put forward as being orders and maps relating to those orders, that is all of the instructions that were given from the staff to the various armies, we are officially asking that your Chamber instruct the Prosecution as quickly as possible to produce those documents and to give them, provide them, to the Defence. We respectfully request the Chamber to do this now and for the following reason: That is, the witnesses we are examining now are, in fact, the witnesses which have to do with the most important shelling. And not putting us -- not giving us that information would not be fair; on the contrary, in the opinion of the Defence, that would be contrary to Articles 21 and 22 of the Statute, which should guarantee that whoever the accused, whatever he be, whatever the crimes alleged, that is the right to have a fair trial. Mr. President, I have finished, and I thank you for listening. I thank you Your Honour for having given me the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do see in the second paragraph of the second page of the letter that the Prosecution has advised the Defence that it will check the material which the Defence has identified in order to confirm that it does not touch upon Sarajevo between April 1992 and September 1994. With what precision you have identified the documents that should be delivered by the Prosecution? I do understand that you say there are certain documents that are of importance for the Defence, say whether they are in the hands of this Prosecution team in this case is not essential. Essentially, it is that they are in the custody of the OTP. Could you tell us with -- is there any misunderstanding as to what documents you are actually referring to? I mean is it -- does Mr. Ierace understand exactly what documents you're talking about? Perhaps I should ask Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer for Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But certainly you'll have --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could imagine, if I have read his letter correctly, that Mr. Ierace knows what we're talking about because he's refusing to give us those documents. Therefore, generally if one says no to something, it means that one understood the question and they would ask you exactly what documents do you want to have. I myself did not personally concern myself with the location of these, the precise description, of those documents. That's my colleague who is here who is responsible for that and she can tell us, if necessary. But I think that the Prosecutor knows what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, it's about how many documents? I'll first ask you how many documents did you identify? Are we talking about 20 or 200 or 2.000?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence can point out that it is -- that it has information that the OTP has all the orders, directives, issued by the Main Staff issued to the Corps. In a letter, my learned friend said that the documents disclosed in this case are not relevant to Sarajevo; however, the Defence points out that these documents, that is, the directives, orders, and commands of the chief staff of the BH army, were sent to all the Corps. And for that reason, the Defence is requesting the OTP to disclose to it all the orders, directives, and commands of the BH army chief staff to the 1st Corps, and also the maps accompanying them which are in the possession of OTP when it comes to the documents of the 1st Corps and in relation to all the brigades of the 1st Corps as well as daily reports. And when I say daily reports, then I can say that these are daily reports which are -- which cover the period between April 1992 to the end of August 1994, or rather the 10th of August, 1994. Likewise, the orders covering this whole period. However, at this point in time, I cannot say how many documents that involves. If my colleagues give me a list of these documents, then we shall be able to know how many of these documents there are, and on the basis of such a list, the Defence could single out the documents that are indispensable to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just put it very bluntly to you: Do you want to have the whole documentary history of the BiH army for the whole period of time irrespective of whether it's about Sarajevo or not? So I would say that the whole conflict, all areas, total of the documentation as far as orders and maps attached to it are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence primarily in relation to the chief staff of the BH army, the Defence primarily wishes to be disclosed all documentation relative to the 1st Corps of the BH army, that is, the main staff of the 1st Corps and all the brigades of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me now turn to Mr. Ierace. I try to understand what the Defence is seeking. Could you please respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it seems from what my learned colleagues have said that they seek documents which emanate from the 1st Corps Main Staff and the brigade which do not relate to the armed conflict in Sarajevo, let alone during the indictment period. In other words, they seek documents which go beyond the scope of the Prosecution case and, in my respectful submission, documents which could not be material to the Defence. One must keep in mind that the subject of the indictment are alleged offences committed by the accused. The Defence has not demonstrated how the documents they seek could possibly be material to the Defence, and I use the word "material" because that is the word contained within Rule 66. Mr. President, I make this broader observation: Last year, the Defence requested various orders and reports of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the period from April 1992 to December 1994. Some months were occupied in exchanges between us in order to refine that period of time. Ultimately that was done. On the date that that material was made available to the Defence in the same letter, they then activated a request for further documents, taking it broader. The Prosecution has done its best to accommodate the Defence reasonably. But this request is, in my submission, well beyond the scope of Rule 66. Mr. President, it is important in my submission that this does not become a dynamic of the Defence having received something, then moves on to something else. Perhaps I could go back to the earlier issue. I will do it very briefly. In today's transcript, at line 25, page 9, Mr. Piletta-Zanin said that he had repeatedly asked the Prosecution for information as to the requests we have made of the Bosnian government authorities for the pieces of shrapnel. If one goes back to the Defence submission of the 5th of March, one will see there is no such request. If one goes to the transcript of the 5th of March, you, Mr. President, specifically asked Mr. Piletta-Zanin whether he had previously asked the Prosecution of the details of the requests made by us for the shrapnel. That appears in the Microsoft Word transcript at page 4.881 and 4.882. You asked Mr. Piletta-Zanin on that; he didn't answer it. You asked him again. He said he would consult with his colleague to find out whether they had previously made such a request. He conferred with his colleague. Again, he did not respond. I am not aware of the Defence having previously made such a request. But Mr. Piletta-Zanin this morning said that he had repeatedly made such requests. Then you, Mr. President, no doubt assuming that that was correct, invited the Prosecution to respond on the spot as to what requests had been made. And you have graciously given us time to do. My point is that the smooth running of this trial depends on a degree of reasonable cooperation between the parties. And in my respectful submission, that is not forthcoming from the Defence at the moment as illustrated by these two issues. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber feels that it wants to take a bit more time to discuss the issue raised and how to proceed in this matter. We'll do that today, but not on this very moment. I think Issue C, the tapes, have been dealt with before. It was my understanding that the Defence at least accepted at that moment that there were no tapes in the custody of the Prosecution concerning any conversations of General Galic, and that's confirmed again in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Two things regarding what I feel like a personal attack; no comment, absolutely no comment. And as for what regards the nonexistence of tapes regarding the conversations, we shall take note of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Before we move to the 92 bis, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if it would assist you, the issue I mentioned before, that was your objection against a question that was leading, I find it in page 5154, line 12 and following. I'll just repeat it to you. The question was: "May I take you, Mr. Sabljica, to the day before the 5th of February, 1994. Now on that day did you investigate another shelling incident." The answer was "Yes." The question was: "Was this in the Dobrinja area?" The answer was: "Yes." And you then made the following objection: "This is a directly leading question, Your Honour. I don't know whether it may be asked. I think the witness should have been asked where it was instead of pointing to it." That was the issue I was referring to, and not anything else. Your response seems to have been on a different issue. This is just in order to assist you in finding it in the transcript. We then move to the 92 bis issue. Before inviting the parties to see whether there's any further comment on what has been exchanged until now in writing, I first have to establish that we have no formal request at this moment to adduce any 92 bis statement, apart from one, and that is the statement of the -- of a deceased witness. But I've seen a request to the Registry. I've seen an exchange of views between the parties. The Chamber has received, although it has not been -- they have not been filed as far as I can see, so therefore the status is a bit uncertain. We have received a lot of documents. Mr. Ierace, after having established this, I'd like to first of all invite the parties to see whether there were any further comments to be made on the 92 bis exercise. Please proceed. Perhaps I give first the floor to Mr. Ierace because he, at least, is responsible for not filing the documents at this moment and being there no formal request. Could you please inform us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Of course we will formally make the application, but clearly the issues can be dealt with in a predetermined fashion at this stage. I do have some additional comments to make. I will be very brief. Firstly, I think that one could divide the witnesses into two categories. The first category are witnesses who essentially attest to the authenticity of certain documents. If I could refer to those witnesses by number, that is the order in which they appear in the binders, they are witnesses 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, and 14, 19, 20, and 21. I have nothing further to add to the written submissions in relation to those witnesses. In my respectful submission, the Trial Chamber will not be unduly troubled by whether 92 bis statements should be accepted from those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you at this very moment, Mr. Ierace, is it your intention to seek permission of the statements and the whole lot of attachments to it? Or do you seek, as you know it's permitted to have a statement partially admitted, just in view of specific items or even specific entries in the documents attached? I mean, you'll understand that if you seek the admission of the whole lot of items, that if for -- just give an example, if one page would be not very well legible, then we would first have to replace that, although it might not be relevant at the end at all. I mean what's the technique you intend to use while formally seeking permission to adduce these documents in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in fact it is just select documents that will be relied upon by the Prosecution rather than the entire collections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I have perhaps one further question to that: Is it your intention to seek permission or only you'll seek permission if the authenticity is made an issue of by the other party? For example, I noticed that at least one of the documents attached to one of the statements has been presented in this courtroom a couple of days ago to a witness. There was no authenticity complained. Would this cause you to refrain from seeking admission, or would you say, no, we nevertheless will -- whatever document has been shown to a witness, we'll seek the evidence as far as the authenticity is concerned to be admitted? So is it just an option if necessary, or do you want to seek the admission of the statements? Have you made up your mind already that you'll seek them all? You mentioned 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 -- 11 or 12 statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, because there are particular annexes to these statements which we'll seek to rely upon, that's probably a better way of putting it, in due course, then it follows that the relevance of those particular annexures will be established first before the Trial Chamber before we then refer to the particular annexia. So clearly, if there is no objection to the tender of, for instance, the medical records for a particular victim, then there is no need for us to rely upon the admission of the 92 bis statement. But if there is an issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- then of course we would leak so rely upon the statement having been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it means that your application will be made whenever it turns out to be necessary because of the objections in respect of the authenticity of the documents presented to a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The difficulty in taking that course is it may result in a hearing of the 92 bis application in chapters rather than in one episode.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And ultimately, that may prove to be inefficient because we would all have to go back to the same arguments. We would have to revisit them. My respectful submission is that it is appropriate that we deal with the admissibility as one episode now, rather than as the situation arises with particular medical records for the reason that ultimately it will be a more efficient way of dealing with the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the other hand, how would you imagine to deal with it in a rather general way? But nevertheless not to cover all the medical records attached because you said, well, only seek admission as far as they relate to specific records. So of course we do not know in advance what medical documents you're going to present to the witnesses, and so we do not know what selection you'll make. And at least until now we've seen not such a selection. If, for example, we have 800 entries in a book with diagnostics or whatever it is, should we go through all the 800 or do you give us your selection or -- you understand if we take a decision, if there's no further specification made, then we take a decision for all 800, then it should be a good decision for all 800. So they should be all legible. They should be all -- it's far easier to concentrate on those that are presented to witnesses unless you have any other evidentiary purposes with these documents. But it it's just authentication of specific medical documents or specific entries in medical records. You understand the problem of the Chamber, which is your problem as well I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps the answer to that dilemma is to determine based on today's argument the issues -- most of the issues which arise in relation to this application. Indeed, all the issues but legibility, that seems to be the primary concern. Therefore, for instance, the Trial Chamber could make a determination which contemplates issues such as the authority of the individual to confirm records. That's one of the concerns to the Defence. And then if it transpires that a particular medical record is illegible, in due course, one that the Prosecution relies upon, illegible to the point that it is not probative, then the Trial Chamber may decline to admit -- either decline to admit that document into evidence; alternatively, if they are admitted at this stage, the Trial Chamber could withdraw that -- allow that tender to be withdrawn or require it to be withdrawn. That, in fact, is available within the Rules. Either way, the issues can be efficiently dealt with today as they pertain to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be another problem as well, that is the following: If we look at the documents, if you would just seek the admission into evidence of the -- well, let's say the authenticity of this document, that this is a document which also appears in hospital X, Y, or Z in the records, then just for these purposes, we would perhaps not need a translation of the document because the only thing we need is to be able to know whether this original document, this copy of a document, is the same as the document that still is in the archives in Sarajevo. As soon as it comes to the content of the document, of course we would need a translation. And therefore, there should always be some kind of a link between specific documents. And we've seen that. Let me just give you an example. We'll see that one of the documents presented to the Witness Boskailo is among the documents, one of the attachments. Of course we received a translation of the document so we could look into the content of the document. Well, there has been no objection against the authenticity, so even without the statement you're now seeking to be admitted into evidence, it was -- the document as such was admitted into evidence. But then, of course, as soon as it comes to presenting the specific document on which you seek now to establish the authentic nature, then of course we come to the content of the document, we would then need a translation. Is that the technique you'd like to use?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. That has always been our intention. In other words, the issue here is whether the document as photocopied is the document which is in the records of the hospital or ambulance station or whatever. That is the ambit of the issue at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand you. But if the document would not be legible, could be not be legible in the original state as well, so that would not, then, perhaps -- should not be a problem or -- I might be afraid that the copying was not done properly or.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's an issue I've referred to two or three times so far in the trial, and I've consistently said that the Prosecution of course must bear the consequences of that. It's apparent to the Prosecution that the originals, in many instances, are not entirely legible. In other words, not 100 per cent of the words in the record are, after so many years after the event, for whatever reason, legible. So from time to time the Trial Chamber will have to, in determining the appropriate weight to be attached to the document, factor into the detriment of the Prosecution on occasions the illegibility of some words or parts of some words. The Prosecution has taken steps to obtain the most legible versions of the documents. I think I've already indicated that a mission was undertaken to Sarajevo in November of last year, whereby an investigator revisited some of these institutions, to obtain more legible copies. In other words, what can be done has been done in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps then you turn to the second category of documents. I'm sorry for interrupting you but I thought it appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll move very quickly through the remaining witnesses. The fifth witness is Sedeta Solak. That relates to scheduled incident number 27. The Trial Chamber has already heard from the investigator of that incident. You may recall that he gave some evidence about a technique involving a tube, how the bullet had penetrated an awning, that is, a bullet fired at the same time, and some glass. In other words, the evidence of that witness will be corroborative not only of the investigator, but also two other witnesses who will be called to give evidence before the Trial Chamber. In that sense, it is corroborative, and I rely in particular upon 92 bis [A], 1 [A], that is a factor in favour of admission is that the proposed evidence is of a cumulative nature and that other witnesses will give or have given oral testimony of similiar facts. This witness is the mother of the boy. Witness number 6, Smail Cekic, the Prosecution will call evidence in due course as to the scope of civilian casualties in the indictment period. There are various sources of material, categories of material available, which are relevant to that issue, some conflicting as to the ultimate figures. This witness, who was the director of a research institute, was involved centrally in administering a questionnaire to household in Sarajevo in April of 1994. There were certain questions in the questionnaire which intended to bring out evidence of civilian casualties. The results of the questionnaire have been collated and they are in the process of being further developed. In due course, an expert witness will give evidence as to that process and the results. But Mr. Cekic's evidence really only goes to the background to the construction and administration of the questionnaire, and that information is contained in his statement. In my submission, that is not or should not be so contentious as to require him to be brought for cross-examination. And it is sufficiently removed from the acts of the accused as to not offend the terms of Rule 92 bis. Next witness I referred to, perhaps I could refer to three together, that's number 12, number 17, and -- at least 12 and 17, are two witnesses who give evidence in relation to what was previously proposed as a scheduled sniping incident, number 1, and now has been descheduled. It is proposed that the victim of that incident, it's a sniping incident, give evidence, and that the statements of these two witnesses -- the third witness is number 7, Deljkovic. So the statements of these three witnesses which are essentially corroborative be given in this form. The witness will give evidence as to where she was at the time she was shot, the direction from which the shot came as she understood it. These three witnesses give some evidence as to known sniping areas at the time and prior to the victim being shot. So essentially it's corroborative. Moving on, number 11, Fahrudin Isakovic, the school principal, I make a point in relation to him and another witness at the same time, that is the last witness, Oystein Strand who was an UNMO on the papa side, that is the Bosnian government side, for four months in 1993. Both of the witnesses refer to the incident that we've already heard about where a school or at least a class was shelled on the 9th of November, 1993, in Alipasino Polje. Mr. President, you and Your Honours may recall that evidence being given about two weeks ago where two shells fell a hundred metres apart both resulting in casualties in that area. I don't rely on that part of the statement for these reasons: He gives a date that is inconsistent, he is a day out, and also inconsistent with the statement of Mr. Strand. And secondly, he was not an eyewitness. It was something he heard about and that he saw on the news that night. The connection is that, of course, the fact that it was an educational institution which was shelled, but we don't require on that particular paragraph of his statement. His evidence is also corroborative in a general sense as to difficulties with schooling. There has been direct evidence before the Trial Chamber from a number of witnesses as to how schooling was disrupted and the difficulties involved in transporting children and the terror which was occasioned to adults and children. Moving on, the next witness I would comment on is number 18, Mr. Celic, who was a victim of the Markale shelling incident. That is also essentially corroborative in its nature. And finally, the second-last witness, Karel Lindr who was an UNMO on the Lima side between May and July 1993. There will be other evidence in the form of UNMOs throughout the period. And in that sense, his evidence is corroborative. And to be candid, he is probably at the other extreme in terms of admissibility. The records from various hospitals being, in my respectful submission, the most conservative aspect of this application. But still within the bounds of 92 bis. Unless there's anything else I can assist Your Honours with, those are my oral comments in relation to the 92 bis. Perhaps just one minor correction to the written submissions, in the second-last paragraph I think it is, there is a word missing. Paragraph 13 in the English version, line 5 from the bottom, sentence reads: "It does mean that the actual content is ultimately true or correct." That should read: "It does not mean that the actual content is ultimately true or correct."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate the page again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, it's paragraph 1 of the response of the Prosecution, that is the response dated the 13th of February, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And the paragraph appears on the -- I think it's the fourth page of the text. It's a little over halfway down that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It does mean that the actual content...it does not mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It should read "it does not mean." There's another error further on in the sentence, but I think that one's apparent. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've perhaps one more question to you, Mr. Ierace. This category of statements, they go to the content of the what the witness said, now and then we see that the statement to the investigator of the OTP refers to an earlier statement given to the authorities of -- well, let's say local authorities. Then we find that there are copies of these statements attached. Is the evidentiary purpose of, that just to establish that a statement was given to the local authorities, or is it also the evidentiary purpose to refer to the content of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It's the latter, Mr. President. Usually, if not in all cases, the context of the reference to the earlier statement is to the effect "I confirm what I have told the earlier investigators." And in that fashion the witness adopts those earlier comments. Where there is not a reference in those terms, that is, confirmation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- it still is nevertheless a document which has emanated either directly or indirectly from the witness and is therefore their account. And by incorporating it in the 92 bis process, having regards to the words of the affirmation, the witness is adopting the contents of the earlier document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would be the intention of the Prosecution to rely on these supporting statements as well, I think in order to understand them, the Chamber would be very much assisted in having translations of these statements as well since you might be aware that the Chamber does not read or understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Mr. President. I had thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no formal application yet. So I said if it would be the intention, then of course we would like to have translations of these as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Certainly that will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having asked clarification on some items --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, just before we move on, I had -- under the check I had done of the binders, I think there were translations for all but one document. And I have translations of that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there were two, but they have not formally been filed, so we never know whether all the binders -- I'm not quite sure that utility binders have exactly the same content. So it would be -- of course I didn't check all the binders of the colleagues and I don't know what has been presented to the Defence. But that's also why my initial -- one of my initial observations was that they have not been filed. And of course there could always be some dispute as to the content of the documents if they have not been formally filed. So we have no formal application yet, so -- but at least you know that what could bother the Chamber if an application would have been made formally with these materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After having asked some clarification to you, Mr. Ierace, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as you've seen, we had some additional questions for Mr. Ierace. We have seen, of course, what his intended application was about, what reasons he gave for it. We of course also have seen that although there was no formal application yet, that you responded already to the idea that the Prosecution would seek admission to adduce these written statements. If there's anything you'd like to add to your written submissions or to what has been clarified today by Mr. Ierace, please do so at this moment. Or of course, Ms. Pilipovic. I should talk to the Defence, but it's so impersonal that either of you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Mr. President, that is usual, our team shares the work because, of course, lady cannot do all the work alone. So of course I will talk of the general context, and Mrs. Pilipovic, who has the art of doing things well, will correct me if you allow me at a later stage. Thank you for giving us the floor, Mr. President. Furthermore, because this is a pilot project in a way, if you will, because the Defence has no knowledge of a decision that would have been taken by one or the other of the Chambers of the Tribunal in relation to a situation which is comparable to this one. There are two reasons for this: First reason being that I belong [sic] that there is no situation, examination of a situation of this extent in Sarajevo. The Chamber has treated other cases other than the direct Sarajevo cases, and the reason -- and another reason for this is the fragmentary character of the structure of the Prosecution. When I say in fragments, I'm not trying to reproach anything to the Prosecution but it is a technique that they are using. They are considering numerous elements in order to put all these fragments together to make a coherent picture. In other words, this is a mosaic technique. If I say this, it's because it does bear a concrete weight. It is important and it is important for this case. Of course I'm not reproaching his Excellency General Galic to having taken a weapon and having acted in a legal sense, but he allowed certain things to happen, presupposing of course that he knew what was going on. So this fragmentary approach of course of the Prosecution makes, Mr. President, the determination of the acceptability, the acceptability of 92 bis much more difficult. Why? Because, in this mosaic vision, if you will, each of the small elements which would be considered as part of a whole will each of these elements will have to be analysed as being something that is directly against General Galic, even if they are small elements, even if some element is small, small in respect of something else, perhaps in a situation of an isolated shooting or an incident at this place or that place. All this put together will be inserted in a large picture in a large mosaic and all this will depict a global picture which we'll have to in the end render your judgment. This is why, Mr. President, we have not up until today seen in the decisions that we have read, for instance in the Sikirica case, and I will repeat for the transcript, Sikirica, or when we talk about other decisions, and I'm thinking here more particularly to -- I'm thinking about the decision entitled Tuta, it is also a decision that is cited in the Sikirica case, and in a decision, in this decision of the Tribunal, we do not see a comparable situation. So far up until today, we have never, this Tribunal has not seen a comparable situation. Mr. President, this being said, I will go back to elements that will be told to you later in writing from the Prosecution, but I would like to point a few things. When we are told that the testimonies would not add anything, would not shed more light or would not add anything to the Prosecution case, meaning that they will have to prove the responsibility of General Galic, but in totality this is not the case, meaning to say that in the totality of most of the cases it is false because we have this mosaic technique that the Prosecution is using and each of these elements have to be taken into account as being an element which can determine the criminal responsibility of General Galic. When we say this, Mr. President, and of course I am referring precisely to point 87 and 8 of the document handed to the Prosecution, the answer of the Prosecution which is not dated February 13th but February 12th, we see very well that the Prosecution is trying to say or is saying that these testimonies would only be corroborative testimonies, that they will only have a corroborative nature. But this cannot be the case. And I would like to remind the Chamber that according to 92 bis, it expressly excludes the admissibility of statements that are filed this way when one tries to prove something that could be directly related to the nature of the indictment against General Galic in our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, exactly indicate where Rule 92 bis says so, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are referring to, but I'm now -- I've got only the English text in front of me. If you're referring to 92 bis [A] where it says the acts and conduct of the accused, I am just wondering what the French version says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Mr. President. I will find it in both languages. But I would like to quote it therefore in French what is allowed, permissible, as to show, and I will quote, to prove a point, other than the actions and the behaviour of the accused such as alleged in the indictment, and we're talking about the Article 92 bis [A] at the end of the first sentence: And it must be the same wording in English that I will find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's perfectly clear. You did not use the words "the acts and the conduct" but that's what you refer to. You used different words, but it's perfectly clear to me now that you refer to the last part of the last line of 92 bis under [A] before the small i's start.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry, Mr. President, but this is what I meant to say. Thank you. If we go back to what we were taking, a certain number of witnesses would only be called, according to the Prosecution, in order to try to determine the origin of fire from the positions held by the SRK. I'm quoting what the Prosecution is saying: "Of fire from SRK positions." The simple fact, Mr. President, that according to this vertical structure, paramedial structure of commandment, to say that the testimonies would only be there to prove the origin of fire from positions held by the SRK meant [sic] position, in other words, held by the Romanija Corps, this would of course imply that General Galic is responsible because he is reproached with the fact of having been a commander there and then. And in this type of statement, we can see that those statements cannot be accepted as having a cumulative factor, but would directly mean that there are some facts that would be reproached to General Galic in those statements. And the same comments can be made also for numerous amount of witnesses that we wish to call, and that the accusation through the Prosecution, and it is obvious and you mentioned, Mr. President, earlier of the authenticity, the question of the authenticity of documents, and we've seen yesterday to what extent it is important that these documents can very often be submitted not only to our cross-examination, but also to the questioning and the cross-examination of the Chamber because there was some translation yesterday that we've seen that were not very satisfying. Mr. President and Your Honours, in all the decisions that we know so far, I have cited two of those earlier, we have -- generally we are dealing with another type of situation. It is a type of a situation where witnesses have already been called and heard before a Chamber of this Tribunal, and witnesses who have already cross-examined either once or more than once. So those are statements of witnesses that are filed and not just simple statements as such. There is a very important difference between the two. There is a difference in the form and a difference at the basis of it. The difference in the form is the following: Formally the statements that would be submitted would be statements in which the person who actually drafted the statements was not called and was not invited to be under oath, to say something under oath according to which the person will tell the truth. And of course the same goes for the interpreters and translators, and this is why I must say that this kind of necessity is important, that this is why when a witness is called to the bar, the witness has to give a solemn declaration. So we have sometimes statements that are not even signed or statements are signed in a language which is not the language of the person that were heard. We have seen the difficulties that this can cause because very often the statements are signed in English, whereas these people who gave the statements do not even speak English. And we can see that this causes an additional problem. But at any rate, the oath is not given and they have not given their oath. And I'm thinking of Cicero who said at the time something like this: The oath is a religious obligation of a religious nature. We do not have any longer any religious obligations of that nature and there is no sermon but there is an oath. And this oath is also very important in view of the general principles. Mr. President, I would like to draw the attention of your Chamber to something I have noticed that the Prosecution took almost half an hour. But I will of course be more brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say I can do it in a couple of minutes, I think we could continue. If not, we would have the break first. So it's not in order to limit you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that maybe it would be perhaps better if we took the break right now, and then we will go on for another ten minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If indeed you will be taking the break now, could I just very briefly say, briefly comment in relation to two matters. I withdraw the application in relation to [redacted]. Steps have been taken for her to attend this week. Therefore we will call her. Secondly, perhaps something to contemplate over the morning break: The Prosecution sought protective measures for [redacted]. That application was dated the 25th of January, 2002. There are some administrative reasons why the Prosecution would be grateful for a response from the Trial Chamber in relation to that application. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the name you just mentioned, we're seeking the protection -- I have to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That has to be redacted. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could I sign the decision -- yes. That will then be redacted. Then we'll have a break until 11.00. Would the parties please -- after the break, the Defence continues what has to be said on behalf of the Defence in respect of what we discussed before. I'd then very much like to hear from you as well, if you're able to do so, any response to the one and only formal application on 92 bis, and that's about the deceased witness, whether the Defence objects or not. Of course you could do it in writing. Still you've got a few days. But if you could express yourself, that would speed up our decision. So if you would please pay attention to that after the break, then we'll now adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before the break, as a result of some email traffic, I informed the Trial Chamber that I withdrew the application for the evidence of Sadeta Solak to be presented by way of 92 bis. During the break, I've learned that the interpretation I placed on the email traffic was incorrect, and I maintain the application by the Prosecution, that her evidence be submitted by way of 92 bis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, I refrained from commenting that since there's no formal application, there's no reason to withdraw, but of course now you still a reason to include her in any formal application you'll make. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think it's up to you to continue your observations in respect of the 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber can be assured that there will not be that kind of problem with the Defence since we don't have an email connection. But having said that, let me go back to where wed left off before the break, Mr. President. I said there were three decisions. I remind you of them. I'm sure you know them. These three decisions might be the closest to what were discussed, and they are the following: The first is the decision called Sikirica, IT-98-1, and then a decision which is known as Natetilic. Also known as Tuta, IT-98-34. And the third is most important, the decision which is known as Delalic, IT-96-21-A, 20-02-01. When we look at those three decisions, we see that there really was no decision which was comparable to the one which we are concerned with today because these dealt mostly with tendering statements which had already been the subject of a solemn declaration, that is to tell the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and statements which are the result of cross-examinations and questions asked by the Chamber itself. Referring to these three decisions, I would like to mention some of the points in them, in particular the decision which I referred to as the Tuta decision, that is, the Naletilic decision. That decision acknowledged that the Chamber could or even should refuse the implementation of the specific procedures of 92 bis when the probative value of the statements was much lower than the need for guaranteeing a fair trial. The English text for that last part of it states: "...to ensure a fair trial." This is the Sikirica decision, which is cited in Tuta at point 6. This need for guaranteeing a fair trial must be analysed in respect not only of the exhibits but also in respect of the situation. Going further, the decision which I've just mentioned stated and recalled that in application of Articles 20, 21 of the Statute, a fair trial must be guaranteed, but especially that Chamber accepted that if the documents at issue could constitute the proof of a critical factor of the thesis of the Prosecution, the cross-examination is necessary. Otherwise stated, the right to a cross-examination could not be refused to the Defence when at issue is admitting an element which could be as stated in the decision the proof -- the proof of a critical element against the accused. This, Mr. President, is where this Prosecution's mosaic-like structure takes on a particular importance, because we must look at that as a totality in respect of the very structure of the indictment as wished by the Prosecutor. The mere fact, for instance, that each time it says that this or that shooting came from this or that area located in a territory under the authority of General Galic is already this type of dalebunte [phone] Therefore in application of the precited decision could not be admitted. What the Prosecution wants is to conceal completely the objective factor of the situation and is trying to dilute the responsibility in some way of the accused in favour of the theoretical admissibility of the facts, even if they were repetitive without the Defence being invited to demonstrate the opposite of what has been said. As regards the decision -- the Delalic decision, I will cite it again, this is one which is 20 February, 2001. Mr. President, Your Honours, there are things which we have learned in this courtroom, in particular at the time of and thanks to the cross-examination. Before I have give the floor to my colleague, I'd like to give some examples that all of us have in mind. We are thinking about the incident Kapor where we saw that in the cross-examination we discovered there was a military objective or target -- target very close to the incident. Here, too, we will -- we found during the cross-examination the presence of an object which is within the very axis of the window with the consequences that that entails, or can entail. I'm referring to your own request dated 4 February 2001 in respect of the documents as stated by Your Honour Judge Orie, and I said relating to these documents which have been produced before the Chamber: "Highly regrettable that there are differences." Let me remind you that there were differences between the English and Serbian language documents and whereas, it was a witness who had signed the statement in a language he had not really understood, that is English, and we are basing ourselves only on those documents. And you pointed out that there were significant differences between the two versions. I would also mention the Witness Mirsad Abdurahmakovic who further to a question asked by Judge El Mahdi allowed us to see that there was near that incident a Golf-type vehicle, in fact, it was a Golf, that was used for moving about the mortars and carry out the firing from that type of car. And then on the 5th and 6th of February, in -- there's another question of translation problems because that witness said that she had never said that her husband had never been a military official or a military commander. And we could mention two other examples, I'm talking now only about an inexhaustive list, the witnesses Kadric, where we saw that there were all the other problems, because those witnesses in the end acknowledged that one of the people it questioned was a military person carrying out a military-type of mission at the time of the incident and as late as yesterday, the taxi driver witness we heard, Mr. Esad Hadzimuratovic, declared that he was a military person and further to a question by the Chamber acknowledge that his civilian vehicle has been used as such during the war by the armed Sarajevo forces. All of this, Mr. President, represent examples only, examples only, but they do demonstrate why and to what extent the cross-examination is something which is absolutely imperative. In a little while, my colleague will tell you that in respect of the witnesses who are in -- going to testify in respect of casualties, how important that testimony is because otherwise we would not have been able to ask questions. In other words and in conclusion, we will speak -- we already mentioned mosaics. But in the -- in painting, there are two very important things, one is what is known as a shortening things, that is to show perspective in a shorter version and then you have a morphosis. That is to show another image than the one looks at the object in front of you. So we have the impression that not only is the Prosecution seeking to establish a kind of mosaic-type work, but also in some ways trying to shorten things using that method so that we don't look at the entire dimension of the matter but to create something which is shortened at the same time that it wants to give to the reality of the facts a distortion, a different vision, of what is at issue. And that is why the Defence cannot accept this and why it objects to the tendering of all of those exhibits covered by those things which are requested by Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I, before your colleague continues, ask whether this would mean that you withdrew the approval of three witnesses in your written observations, your written submissions, I find that you agreed with three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, I was carried away. Not necessarily. We insist on all of our conclusions, and that also includes these three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you for giving the Defence the floor at this point in time and allowing my colleague and me, representing the Defence, to say certain things which we believe are of fundamental importance with regard to the application of Rule 92 bis. First I'd like to add that in our application of the 4th of February, which was submitted to the Chamber and the reasoning of the Defence, that in it we said that three witnesses for whom our learned friends want to tender death certificates from Sarajevo, we said that we were agreeable to tendering these three death certificates, but we also point out that these death certificates can prove that somebody has died but not how that person died, because these documents do not indicate the cause of death. And I'd also like to refer to the quality of evidence submitted to us by the Prosecution with these death certificates, and we can see how -- we cannot see how authentic these documents are because the law envisages -- the law defines what is the proof of death, and we have already said that it was a death certificate from the Book of Deaths. But otherwise, the notification of that does not quote the cause of death and the fact of death. So this is the view of the Defence with regard to documents and admission of statements of three witnesses through which our learned friends wanted to produce the death certificates, that is, we question the quality of this evidence which will no doubt add to the overall load of this case. What the Defence also wishes to point out and to touch upon is a submission which my learned friends filed to respond to the Defence's response regarding Rule 92 bis. Under Item 4 of this submission, our colleagues say that the production of evidence under 92 bis is based on the wish to expedite the proceedings and that in such a case, the Chamber should be allowed to admit the statements of the witnesses who are not proving acts and conduct of the accused with which General Galic is charged. In Item 4, they are referring to Judge Hunt's decision in the Vasiljevic case, IT-98-32-T of the 17th of September 2001. We wish to say the Defence has nothing against saving time, but likewise, we wish to say that the economy of time cannot be at the expense of justice and fair trial to which General Galic is entitled. We wish to point out that in this case, the Prosecution sets out to prove General Galic's guilt, responsibility, whereas the indictment does not describe a single act of the accused which the Prosecution sets out to prove, and it resorts all the time to circumstantial evidence. We therefore point out that there is no difference between witnesses we have heard so far and who have appeared in this Court and those witnesses whose statements the Prosecution wishes to introduce by way of Rule 92 bis. So why do these witnesses need to personally appear here, both Mrkovic and Dzubur Ferhazeta and Deljakovic Alije and Isakovic Fahrudin and Brkanic Hamdo and [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters unfortunately do not have the lists of names of these witnesses. And they therefore apologise for their mispronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in order to be able to -- in order to solve the problem of names, I shall try to mark them with numbers, except that I do not have at hand the submission with numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would it be possible that you provide to those who work on the transcript in the evenings a list of the names you just mentioned so that they can check while listening to the tape what names you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I can supply the list of these witnesses later except that these witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I won't repeat them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please do that not later, but approximately at the end of today's session. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Therefore, why is it necessary for all these witnesses to appear before this Court? Although the Defence will indicate broader relations concerning every one of these witnesses and we did so in our application of the 4th of February, 2002, we wish to say that in those statements all these witnesses speak about events in which individuals were injured, and in some of these statements, they speak very vaguely about incidents, and they do not know when they happened, where they happened, who was involved in these incidents. And it is, therefore, necessary to question these witnesses directly. And my colleague has said in his presentation, has analysed several witnesses in his presentation and explained why his direct examination was necessary and also why the Defence should be enable to cross-examine them. We also wish to point out that if the Prosecution wishes to -- that is, if it wishes to introduce the statements of the witnesses in line with the 92 bis and to prove the scope and the number of casualties, then obviously it has to do with what the General Galic is charged with here. Therefore, we think that the Prosecution should not be allowed to produce such evidence without enabling the Defence to check who is the victim, whether this victim was possibly a member of the armed forces, or other forces taking part in armed operations or contributing to such operations without enabling it to establish where and when such incidents happened, as well as other facts of relevance for the verification of credibility of these witnesses, because the credibility of these witnesses whose statements would be introduced in line with 92 bis in no way can be verified which is absolutely always goes to the detriment of the accused himself, and also affects the fairness of the trial. The Defence can say that if the Prosecution believes that saving of time is of primary concern, the Prosecution can save time by not calling these witnesses or using their statements. I'd merely like to say a few words to mention how worried is the Defence when 92 bis is applied to a (ii). It has to do with the statement which the Prosecution wishes to produce, and these are the statements of Alisa Deljkovic and Mrkovic, and Cankovic. We heard today that our learned friends wish to call here as a witness a lady for whom protection measures were sought and who will appear as a witness, who was a victim of an incident. The Prosecution claims that it happened on the 7th of November, 1992, and that incident is not covered by the list of incidents. First, we wonder whether the Prosecution is allowed to produce in evidence before this Court in view of the decision of Judge Rodrigues, that the introduction of new incidents in the evidence is not introduced, but even if we take that the Prosecution is allowed to do that, but then the Defence is also entitled to cross-examination. In other words, we are worried by such a solution, that is, that the Prosecution can introduce circumstantial evidence in this manner without, however, introducing any evidence through direct and immediate examination. The Defence should like to point out in particular the production of statements of witnesses as to circumstances about which some witnesses have already testified. In other words, here the question arises concerning the production of statements of Salko Zametica, Brkanic Hamdo, Mr. Strand, Mr. Lindr Karel. All of them in their statements speak about sniping and shelling incidents, and they speak about them as eyewitnesses. For these reasons, the Defence needs to cross-examine them. Likewise, my learned friend, in his opening address, said why Srdjan Cankovic need not to be examined directly and personally. The Defence points out that in his statement, Mr. Mersockavic [phoen] Also refers to incidents which are not attributed, that is snipings and shellings, and during the period of time for which Mr. Galic is charged. We are particularly worried when it comes to Celic's statement. He was an eyewitness to an incident and who was wounded on that occasion; that is, I go back to the Defence's position which I've already explained at the outset, that it is necessary to examine -- to call all these witnesses to appear in person because the Defence needs to be given the possibility to directly hear these witnesses. As for the medical documentation, I'd merely like to point out, and it says so in the record, that medical documentation is illegible, that copies are such that one cannot establish matters of relevance for the case. That is, the medical documentation does not lend itself to complete verification; that is, one cannot establish what kind of injury, what kind of type because the copies are illegible, and they are simply unacceptable. Yesterday, we were all in a situation to see how important it is to see the original of a document and how useful original documentation can be. And another thing I wish to point out is the death certificates and medical documentation which the Prosecution wishes to introduce via Rule 92 bis, and let me quote Witness Safeta Krestalica, through this witness, the Prosecution wishes to introduce the documentation covering the period of 1995 and November of 1994. Likewise, through other witnesses, there is a great deal of medical documentation which is not relevant for the period that we are talking about here. In other words, I wish to emphasise once again that it is in the interests of justice and fair trial that the written application -- that the introduction of statements by way of Rule 92 bis be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence still owes you an answer regarding the introduction of the statement of the late Hamdija Cavcic. The Defence objects to the admission of this statement because this, again, runs counter to Rule 92 bis [A] since to admit somebody's statement and to assess the testimony of a witness, such testimony needs to be subjected to cross-examination, and we are unable to do that because Mr. Cavcic died. And we, however, object that this statement be admitted in evidence under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are referring to 92 bis [A], or...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In this statement, in Mr. -- statement of -- to put it that way -- late Mr. Cavcic refers to incidents and facts which are relevant for the period that General Galic is charged. That is why we are against the admission of the statement, because the Defence is unable to -- because the Defence cannot subject the statement to cross-examination. In the statement which was disclosed to the Defence, one reads about acts and conduct of the accused. And for this reason -- I'm looking at the Rule 92 [C]. Evidently, that is the rule that is referred to by my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, by referring to Rule 92 [A] I do understand that you take the position that all the requirements of 92 [A] have to be fulfilled, although the form 92 [B] prescribes might not be fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, unless there's something very critical to respond to, I would rather close the debate on this issue. But I'll give you opportunity to touch upon --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's nothing I wish to add about the 92 bis argument. I simply say that -- say this, however: My friend mentioned the status of the sniping incident which I described as previously sniping incident number 1. And my friend said that it was troubling that we were leading evidence on that contrary to the judgment of the Pre-Trial Chamber. In fact, in that judgment, the Pre-Trial Chamber expressly allowed us to lead evidence in relation to that incident, and the witness who we are calling, who was the victim, is the subject of a 65 ter summary. So my friends should not be caught by surprise for both those reasons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Ms. Pilipovic, I'd rather --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I've just explained why all these witnesses should be cross-examined. I believe I've understood what my learned colleague has just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
