utterances.text: Mr. President, there is the matter of Mr. Cavcic. I did not make that the subject of any submissions. If the Trial Chamber requires some submissions from the Prosecution in relation to the admissibility of that statement, then I'd be happy to provide that or Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we think we need any further clarification in that respect, we'll ask for it, Mr. Ierace. Let me just close this debate on 92 bis, which was a bit of an odd debate because it was without any application formally made. But that's what we can expect soon I take it, from the Prosecution. I'd like to stress that the Chamber would be very pleased to have a thoroughly structured application, not a kind of puzzle where we have to find whether all these statements in the Eta station are also attached to the Eta station where we have to wonder whether those not attached would not be part of the application and -- well, I indicated already similar issues like any attached document not being translated, would it serve the evidentiary purpose of the content or just of the existence of the statement. So therefore, the Chamber would very much like to have all these aspects clearly set out in the application, then of course the application to be accompanied by all the documents necessary for us to decide. And I made a few observations as well on the issue of medical records and whether all of them were relevant or part of them were relevant, how to introduce them. Of course, we leave it to the Prosecution. But well-structured application is very much preferred by the Chamber. Also, and that's the second observation I'd like to make, that we'll have to apply Rule 92 bis in -- which is especially paragraph A is of major importance for the decision. The Defence has already pointed to -- let me just try to summarise it, what they call the critical elements, and they also made reference to the acts and the conduct of the accused, because that in its literal wordings is one of the criteria that is mentioned in 92 [A]. The Chamber also thinks that this is very important to be precise on this criteria in view of the charges brought against the accused, which are to some extent charges under Article 71, and on the other hand, charges under Article 73. And I can imagine if you are talking about the acts and the conduct of the accused, that it might be of some importance to differentiate between whether you are talking about Article 71 charges or Article 73 charges. I'm not going to tell the Prosecution what they should include in their application, but -- well, some problems were raised in this courtroom, and the only thing I'd like to stress is that apart from a solid structure, that proper attention is paid to all the legal problems attached to the application of Article 92 bis in this specific case. I'll leave it to that unless, Mr. Ierace, you'd like to ask or comment on anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have two points of clarification. Given that we are required to file multiple copies of the statements as part of our formal application, might I inquire whether the Trial Chamber requires multiple copies of the attachments? Because they are, indeed, voluminous, in particular the attachments to the statements of recordkeepers. Would it be acceptable to file less than the usual required number of annexures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We even have been considering another solution, and that is to return the binders to you, take out all comments we did write in it, and provide you with -- I'm just talking for the Judges -- nine binders, documents, still clearly identifiable to what statement they relate. If that would be a solution so that we have it nicely structured and you also the copies already made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, Mr. President. That would be a great help. The second question relates to your observations in relation to 71 and 73, and the first part of 92 bis. Do I understand you, Mr. President, to be inviting some further submissions in writing from the Prosecution accompanying the formal application, and those submissions would canvass or perhaps even recanvass the basis upon which the Prosecution submits the statements are admissible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the Defence made objection specifically -- they have given their view on how the phrase "acts and conduct of the accused" should be understood when applying Rule 92 bis. I can imagine that your view on the structure of the charges, I mean, it has been explained by the Defence on how they look at these charges and what the structure is and what -- perhaps if supplying the Chamber with an answer or your views, perhaps your differing views, on that issue, that it might assist the Chamber to come to a quicker decision on the application and would prevent us from, in a second round, ask for clarification of these issues. And I just identify a few who seem to be of a rather key importance in the view of the Defence for the decision to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. President. I'm led to believe that there will be a judgment delivered in the next week or so from one of the other Trial Chambers on 92 bis. If it's convenient, I'll wait until that judgment comes down because I could then incorporate it in those submissions if you would assisted by that, or would you prefer that we proceed immediately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me give you an answer to that after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Perhaps before -- well, if you're going to confer, before you give your opinion, would you allow me to give the Defence position in respect of some of the points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first thing I did, as a matter of fact, is to see whether we would deal with it at this moment or at a later stage. And of course you have the opportunity to give your observation, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You can do it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll do it in a little while, Your Honour. A little while. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber as such has no problem to wait until the decision is granted. So unless the Defence would come up with some objection which would convince us that you would have to do it earlier, you may wait until next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There was also another issue that you indicated you would like dealt with this morning. That was the expert witnesses. Do you still wish me to throw some light on that issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let me just first see what Mr. Piletta-Zanin has to... Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. You would note that the Defence has prepared itself, depending on what the Prosecution planned to submit or not to submit, and therefore we have based our resources on the procedure which the Prosecution wants and not based on anything else. And this means that if, by chance, we were to agree that the Prosecution can again file new submissions on that same subject, it is clear that the Defence should first be so informed and to prepare itself accordingly. That seems clear to me. I regret personally that this was not done all at once, but it is clear that our position will be to state clearly that we must know how the Prosecution intends to complete its points each time, and if necessary, to take a position against that. That's one point. The second point in respect of the decision that will come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you a question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The submission you just made, is that in relation to 92 bis? Yes, that's clear to me now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bis [A]. I'm talking about that. And we should be invited to take a decision, because this opportunity has been offered by your Chamber to the Prosecution. The other point, Mr. President, is to review whether or not it is necessary to wait until the decision mentioned comes -- is issued. The decision which the Prosecution mentioned a little while ago. What I mean by this is as far as the Defence knows, no decision has come about, unless we're talking about the Milosevic trial, and in that case we would find ourselves in an identical position. If it isn't part of the Milosevic trial, I don't think that we're talking about a comparable situation, that is, the production of statements of people who were not heard previously as witnesses. That is an essential factual distinction between the two situations, that is, persons who have been heard orally and those who have not according to the rules. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...disclose to us in what case you expect a decision or is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The situation is that it involves a confidential judgment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll not -- would there be a problem to -- perhaps you need it commissioned first from the other Chamber to even in private session to disclose to the Defence in what case it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. I anticipate there will be a redacted version made public in the next week or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then you'd provide the Defence with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd then like to close the debate on the 92 bis issue. What is still there is the expert witnesses. We heard something about it from Mr. Stamp last week, I think, although perhaps not in every detail. And there's another issue, there's the request from the Defence to give orders in respect of the orders, the military orders, and the documents containing military orders and eventually maps attached to it. Perhaps since we dealt with it this morning, we'll deal with that first. Perhaps, Mr. Ierace, may I just first ask for a clarification in respect of the letter you -- or the response you gave to us this morning which you said you filed yesterday. On the first page, last paragraph, it reads: "At subsequent meetings with the Defence, the Prosecution made clear that it has disclosed the existence of the relevant ABiH orders and reports." Did you disclose merely the existence of the relevant orders or did you also disclose the orders themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution made available to the Defence the index of the orders that we possessed and invited the Defence to select from that index the documents which they -- which they wished to have copies of. And that was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I also do understand by now that the Defence takes the position that in other cases, orders have been admitted into evidence, orders which do not appear on the list and of which you say they are not in any relation to Sarajevo and are therefore irrelevant and of which the Defence says that they are material to the Defence. And I also see that on the second page, that you've indicated to the Defence that you'll check the material which the Defence has identified in order to confirm that it does not touch upon Sarajevo between April 1992 and September 1994. This means that there is a dispute as to the materiality of these documents for the Defence. At this very moment, the Chamber gives no specific orders given the undertaking of the Prosecution to check the material any further. Am I right in understanding, then, if you check this material, that you'll come up with some kind of a list, present it to the Defence so that the Defence could indicate that documents on this list, even if, perhaps, not on earlier lists, are material and for what reasons they are material to the Defence? Is my understanding right that it would take you a couple of weeks to prepare that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would not propose to include our explanation as to why it is material to the Defence or why it may be material to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but the Defence can of course comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So I would provide an index of any documentation which is relevant to what occurred in Sarajevo between April of 1992 and September of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber wonders -- first of all, may I ask you, as we are talking about orders from the General Staff, and we heard a distinction made between orders by the General Staff of the BiH army generally addressed to I would say all parts of the army, and those specifically given to the 1st Sarajevo Corps. Two questions in that respect: The first one is, were all orders given to the Sarajevo Corps disclosed to the Defence as far as they are in your custody or under your control?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would feel more comfortable if I had a little time to make some further inquiries before I responded to that. But my understanding is that we have searched only for documents which relate specifically to the Sarajevo campaign, rather than documents which relate more broadly to the 1st Corps. And that is because of the words material to the Defence which occur in Rule 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. I also understand that there's as a matter of fact the dispute where -- are all orders to the 1st Sarajevo Corps relevant for the situation in Sarajevo, or just those specifically dealing with the campaign as it appears in the indictment in Sarajevo at the relevant time. We feel that there are general orders given to all parts of the army, which would include, although not specifically addressed to the 1st Sarajevo Corps, and we see other orders that might be specifically given to the 1st Sarajevo Corps. Of course, the problem of the Chamber but also the problem of the parties is that if you do not know the content of the orders, it's not easy to assess how material they are. I mean, it's still possible that something happens at a distance of 200 kilometres, but which might be of major importance for what happened in Sarajevo. That's -- I'm just talking on a general level. I'm not on any specific issue. Because we would expect that general orders that were given to all parts of the army, including the 1st Sarajevo Corps, might be relevant as well. I say "might be relevant as well." I don't know whether they are relevant or not. That's the first issue. And the second one is what kind of orders are there which, as you say, are not specifically related to the charges but are addressed to the 1st Sarajevo Corps might be relevant as well. I'd rather try to see what kind of lists you can produce, what lists you already produced, and then see whether the Defence is able to indicate what the materiality of these documents for the Defence would be, just as I would expect from the Defence that when they identified any specific documents that have been produced in other trials, that they would indicate clearly to the Prosecution what documents they are referring to. May I just give the opportunity now to Mr. Piletta-Zanin to...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And for two reasons I thank you. One, for giving me the floor. First, I would like to assist the Prosecution and say that the Defence will give an answer to the question you asked, and that's the following: No. All the orders dealing with the 1st army were not disclosed to the Defence. That's the first point. The second point is the list of orders, it is difficult for us in this disorder -- I don't want to use that word but I'll say it anyway -- it is difficult for us in this disorder to get this kind of list because we're talking about material that the Prosecution has in its possession, and therefore it's difficult to get the indications. But what is more important is this: It is only once we have seen the contents of these orders that we will be able to determine clearly with our experts as to the relevant or less relevant content of those orders. The first step is to provide them to us. It will be a great deal of work for the Defence, but it will do the work and depending on what we find, we will say this is pertinent, relevant or not. However, this is not done, and I see apparently one doesn't want to do this. The Defence is put into a position where it cannot cross-examine the witness normally because important information might be lacking, information that it might have found in the documents which are now in the possession of the Prosecution. So we can try to cooperate with the drawing up of lists. We are willing to do that. But to compare a complete exhaustive list is something we cannot do, not because we don't want to, but because the information physically is somewhere, somewhere to where we do not have access. I think there's nothing further to add to that, and once again, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we see, as a matter of fact, is that we have to draw a line between what would in the end turn out to be a fishing expedition on the one hand other, and on the other hand side, what would be a reasonable effort in order to disclose to the Defence what the Defence would need to properly defend the accused. That's not easy. I gave some observations. I see that the Prosecution is making new efforts in order to see whether we can proceed on this issue. I'll not give any specific orders at this time, but I think there's still some fruits to be expected from exchange of view between the parties. We would like to be informed immediately again if this would not result in any progress in reaching an agreement on what could be expected from the Prosecution to additionally find out and where the wishes of the Defence reach a point where we would say this is too large, this is too broad, we cannot expect the Prosecution to put more efforts in that. May I -- you said it would take you another couple of weeks to complete what you intend to do. May I just first invite the parties to discuss this matter again and inform the Chamber, but then -- well, let's say in not more than five minutes any dissatisfactory development in these discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I suggest an alternative course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You directed two specific questions to the prosecution whether we have disclosed orders which relate to the army as a whole and secondly whether we have disclosed or made available the orders, all of the orders of the 1st Corps. Naturally both of those are qualified by the documents we have, rather than those that might exist somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It may be beneficial if I respond to those specific questions, say, on Friday morning, and that may be a helpful step in defining any further search that should be conducted. I say that because if the Trial Chamber takes the view ultimately that further documents should be disclosed, it would be helpful to the Prosecution to know that before we finalise the search which we are presently doing. And it's apparent to me that the gulf between the Prosecution and Defence on this issue really will probably require some direction from the Trial Chamber. So if we do that first, then perhaps we can crystalise what remaining dispute there is. It shouldn't take me long on Friday morning to inform the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have now more or less identified the problem and drawn the attention to some aspects of it. And I think, having not given any orders at this moment, it would be fair that you have an opportunity next Friday morning to inform the Chamber in further detail, and then see whether any order is still sought or how to proceed on from Friday morning. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, thank you, Mr. President. It is being stated that Friday morning, I may unfortunately not be here, because that is the 15th and I had scheduled something else. If I can get free, I will be here. But if I can't, I won't. We'll try to get closer to the Prosecution for the umpteenth time, and if I could make some suggestions, the Prosecution should open its files to us and show us the documents, show us the orders and we could say prima facie this is of interest to us, we don't have it. This is of interest to us and so on. It's a simple exercise. It would take a few hours but we would find after the hearing and we would move forward very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...on the basis of reciprocal disclosure that whatever documents are in the custody of the Prosecution, you'll be allowed to inspect them. Am I wrong in my understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: With respect, Mr. President, you are wrong because we are confined by the words in the Rules, "which are material to the preparation of the Defence." And this is the difficulty: My friend cannot demand these documents without explaining how they are material to the Defence. One has regard to the pretrial brief from the Defence, and when one looks at that document filed by the Defence, it is not clear at all how these documents relate to that Defence. But I'll take the first step in the next few days. I appreciate my friend will not be here on Friday. I'll attempt to do it on Thursday morning, but then the ball passes to my friend to explain how these documents are material to the Defence filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course then the problem is he can only do it in general wordings since he has not seen the documents and that's the dilemma we're in and that's also the difficulty to draw a line between a fishing expedition and what I said before, what would be a reasonable request from the Defence to have additional documents disclosed. I'll then disclose this debate, and we'll then proceed later on -- and we still have the -- after the break, yes. That would be -- we'll have a break at half past 12.00. We have three minutes left. Would that be enough for the experts, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll do my best. I'll move through them fairly quickly, Mr. President. I have before me the names and categories which you identified on the 5th of March. So going through that list, the first name that you identified, Mr. President, was Commander John Hamill, who is an UNMO, and you wondered whether he is being called as an expert. He is not. The 65 ter summary refers to two areas where at that stage we contemplated he would give evidence. The first was the role he played in the preparation of the United Nations' report on Markale. The second was in relation to the first scheduled shelling incident, the football game at Dobrinja. The Prosecution will not lead evidence from him in relation to the first scheduled incident, only in relation to Markale. The Prosecution calls him to explain what he did and to confirm the conclusions which he arrived at in the report in relation to Markale. Now that report was prepared for the United Nations, not for the Prosecution and the Tribunal, and that is the important distinction in determining whether he is called now by the Prosecution as an expert witness. I should say that generally in relation to each of these individuals, the Rules, in particular 94 bis, contemplates that some witnesses are called as experts, but in fact many witnesses who are called by the Prosecution and the Defence in the Tribunal in effect give expert evidence on various points. And from time to time they have to be qualified before they can give that opinion, whatever it is. So really what we're talking about is a more fundamental distinction between who is an expert and who is not. Moving on, the second name that was mentioned was Sabljica, and of course that has been dealt with. The next one was Higgs, warrant officer Higgs. There was a 65 ter summary for him which identifies him as an expert in relation to mortars, and he is an expert for the purposes of 94 bis. A report is in the process of being prepared, and I anticipate that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will slow down. I anticipate that -- indeed, it has been filed. Therefore, I move on. Richard Philips will be an expert of the analyst type. We will comply with Rule 94 bis in relation to his evidence. Likewise, Dr. Turner, and we have already done so in relation to Robert Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Witness AD, we have discussed earlier. That's now Witness Q, although the relevant 65 ter summary is listed under the name "Witness AD." The evidence of that witness falls into the same category of that of Commandant Hamill, that is he is not an expert in relation to 94 bis, but rather who will give evidence as to findings which he came to on earlier relations in relation to scheduled and unscheduled incidents. We then move to Ismet Cekic. I discussed him in a different capacity earlier this morning and for the same reasons that I advanced on that occasion, I say that he is not being called as an expert witness. I referred earlier to there being a statistics expert who would be called to give evidence in relation to the collated results of that questionnaire and some other material. That witness has been identified by the Prosecution and is in the process of preparing a report. There is a considerable volume of material to be processed and to be referred to in the report. And it is probably still some weeks before that report will be filed pursuant to 94 bis. Mr. President, you also referred to the 65 ter summary for sniping expert. That witness has been identified and is in the process of preparing his report. I wish that witness to have available to him in summary form the evidence of the witnesses who the Prosecution has called and will be calling in relation to the scheduled sniping incidents. Therefore, his report will not be ready until those witnesses have all been called. I anticipate he will give evidence towards the end of the trial. And through him also will come some maps of each of the sniping incidents with expert evidence as to the distances. Those distances are being obtained by the use of professional instruments. I should also indicate that I anticipate the Prosecution will seek leave to add a further name for the witness list in relation to the preparation of the maps, that is, the maps for each of the sniping and shelling incidents, to give evidence as to how those maps were developed and determined. I move on to the 65 ter summary for the artillery expert. In a similar fashion, we're not likely to tender that report until towards the end, perhaps after the end, of the shelling component of the trial. There were two entries, 65 ter summaries, for ballisticians. One is described as a ballistic physicist and the other as a ballistician. We will combine those into one expert, that is, a ballistician. The evidence of that witness will pertain largely if not entirely to the Markale market incident. Mr. President, that leaves one, perhaps two, witnesses. The command and control expert and Rick Butler. There was some discussion of Rick Butler's status and report timetable on the 5th of March. There's nothing further I can add today to that. The command and control expert will have access to the report of Rick Butler, and therefore of necessity, must follow him. As well, it makes good sense for the command and control expert to have regard, at least in summary form, to much of the evidence which the Trial Chamber is hearing. And therefore, his testimony and his report of necessity must come at the very last stage of the trial. We are working on that. So, Mr. President, essentially most of the witnesses will be treated by the Prosecution as 94 bis witnesses, except with the exceptions I have already mentioned in terms of a list of names that you provided. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification, Mr. Ierace. I think that we then dealt with all the subjects that were still pending at this very moment, and that after the break, we can resume the examination of the witness Mr. Sabljica. We'll then adjourn until five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say good morning, Mr. Sabljica but unfortunately I have to say good afternoon. We apologise, but it took us a long time this morning to deal with some legal issues we had to deal with first. So you had to wait. I indicated to the Victims and Witness Unit that it would not be at 9.00. I hope that this message came to you. Mr. Ierace, I see that you're standing, where I expected Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, I would like to make two very quick points in relation to those earlier topics and then I will lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll see that I tried to finished before the break. But just briefly check. One more moment, Mr. Sabljica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I addressed the issue of Mr. Cekic. I should also say in relation to Mr. Ceric because he was the psychiatrist who is not being called by the Prosecution as an expert witness according to 94 bis. That's my first point. And secondly, in relation to expert reports generally, where they are filed and subsequent evidence is contradictory to the presumptions of the report, then of course the Prosecution will file an amendment or invite the expert witness to amend his conclusions accordingly, if that is required. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wanted to draw the attention of the Prosecution to the fact that if we grant names or if we say names rather, it is better not to say them out loud in front of witnesses. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In general I would agree with you. I don't think that any harm was done at this very moment. Then, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Sabljica, may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday. You'll not find any screen behind you because the situation in this courtroom is different from what it is in the other courtroom. But the protective measures are still effective. Yes, please, Mr. Stamp. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. May I proceed, may I just inquire if the Court has a record of how long I have been in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't got it in my mind. I'm sure Madam Registrar could present it to you. Please proceed. As soon as Madam Registrar -- we have to check it, I think, from yesterday's transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said last time that the investigating magistrate would be one of the persons responsible for checking casualties. Could you, from your record in respect of the incident of the 4th of December, 1994, tell us who that investigating magistrate was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness, with your leave, Mr. President, be handed Exhibit P2247A.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigating magistrate in this case was Mr. Zdenko Eterovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a matter of clarification before I go on, in respect of the incident of the 5th of February, 1994, in which direction is Marsal Tito Street in respect to the Markale market, to the north, south, east, or west?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In respect to the Markale market, the street Marsal Tito is situated south of the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. President, with your leave, may I proceed to show the witness a video which have been produced by the Defence to the Court but which we have given to the Defence. It is marked D64.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you... Yes, D64. Mr. Stamp, meanwhile, I can inform you that it's a bit over two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I beg your pardon, Mr. President. I am indeed very mindful of that because we have witnesses here, and next week we have obligations in respect to the videolink, so we need to dispose of these witnesses who are here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Registrar. We have the video ready to be played? Yes, I see it's on our screen now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I ask that we start again. I'm afraid I didn't...I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Stop here, please. Could you take it back just a little. And stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The gentleman on the right, could you say who that person is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm terribly sorry to interrupt, but we have seen on another cassette video that at times, we can see conversations, or there's an exchange between different people who are filmed. These exchanges are very often important for the case. I do not know if the interpreters can hear those conversations that are taking place. If they hear them well enough, I was wondering if they could interpret. I don't really know what means the interpreters have, but this is a suggestion perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. First of all, Mr. Stamp, you're using the video now. Is it about the pictures or is it about the conversations?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm using the video to show images, Mr. President, and I am trying to move pretty quickly. I would ask if there is anything in respect to what is said on the videos, I would like it to be inquired about during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you can do it during cross-examination, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who is that person on the screen to the right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please proceed with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The blackening and burning that is depicted on this frame, could you be briefly describe what it is or what would have caused it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was caused by a projectile, a mortar shell, that fell right next to that wall. So we see the damage caused to the wall. It is the fragments of the grenade that caused this damage, and you can see parts of earth and mud and the fumes coming out from gun powder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you stop there, please. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you describe what you see in that frame, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this photograph, we can see the stabiliser of the mortar shell, the calibre is 120 millimetres. It is embedded in the centre of the crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you stop here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You had indicated what this was in respect of the photographs. But can you observe the stabiliser fin of the mortar round in this photograph, in this frame?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is clearly seen right here, right under the map of the city. Right above it, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see to the right of the compass the arrow that you had placed there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a white arrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you observe any comparison between the angle in which the mortar fin is embedded in the ground and the direction in which the arrow points?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we have a problem here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the technical booth solved the problem meanwhile. I see on many screens around me the picture we last had. Would you please then answer the question of Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The angle under which the tail of the projectile was found is not relevant with regards to the direction of the -- the direction from which the projectile was fired. What is really important is to see all the traces that are present on the asphalt, and this determines the way it fell on the asphalt, determines the direction from which it came.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you recall viewing the photographs of the mortar crater in respect of the Markale incident. And in that incident, you pointed out to where there was a tunnel in which the stabiliser fin was embedded. Here it seems a little bit more exposed. Can you comment on that. Is it unusual or is it something you see occasionally in the many cases that you've investigated?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the examination, you have to take into account the surface on which the projectile falls. It did happen that during some examinations we were able to find remnants of projectiles or a projectile. Precisely in this position as we see it on this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it, then, that on occasion you may find it in a similar deeply embedded position as you saw it in the pictures in respect to the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. There are other factors that come into play right here, but we did not examine them in our reports, such as the angle under which the projectile fell and similar criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But what I'm asking, is it unusual or is it uncommon for sometimes the stabiliser fin to be deeply embedded and sometimes it may not be as deeply embedded as it is in this frame? Does it vary?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not unusual. It does vary, as I said. It depends of the surface on to which the projectile fell, and there are also other factors that one could take into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we proceed with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you stop here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That area to the top right of the screen beyond those two individuals, is that the parking garage that you refer to in your report?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is actually a garage, municipal garage. It is not a parking garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Stop there, please. Just a little bit back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Perhaps before we go any further, for the transcript, could Mr. Stamp please say what is mentioned -- what is on page 74 and onwards so that we can find it in the transcript, in relation to the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might be difficult now to go back to the whole tape. What we see at this very moment is time indicated on the tape, 13.51. And as far as I can see, there was no interruption in playing the tape backwards for some five or six minutes, so that perhaps could identify what was on the tape. And at this very moment, we see in the -- at the bottom of the screen we see what seems to be a map and a compass, and the time at this moment is 13.51 indicated on the screen. I think this would assist whoever will look at the transcript later on and...but perhaps, Mr. Stamp, it is true that if you now and then indicate what you see on the screen, unless it's just running and if you pay no specific attention to any of the issues on it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the bottom of the screen, you see a map of Sarajevo with your compass on it.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is beside a crater with a stabiliser fin in it.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the shell stabiliser is embedded in the centre of the crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And beside it a number 1 placed on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that the crater at the edge of the asphalted area which you referred to in your report?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please proceed with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you stop now, please. Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sabljica, if I could turn your attention a little bit further back in time and proceed to the 22nd of January, 1994. On that day, did you investigate any particular shelling incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say where it was that you investigated this shelling incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Alipasino Polje locality, on the corner of Cetinska and Klare Zetkin Street, and around the Rade Konicara square. But these are old street names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you went there, I take it, with a team of investigators?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and my senior colleague, the late Borislav Stankov was another ballistics man on the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did yourself and Mr. Stankov conduct ballistic examinations and analyses on -- of the shelling incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did Mr. -- did you prepare a report in respect of the shelling incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did it together, Mr. Stankov and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall who signed the report after you prepared it together?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stankov.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, if you saw that report again, would you be able to identify it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, could the witness be handed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, would you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Exhibit P2171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And for the record, the translation is P2171.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That document that you have in front of you, is that the report prepared by yourself and Mr. Stankov and which was signed by Mr. Stankov?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Quickly looking through that report, how many shells did you investigate?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three shells, and we found one stabiliser, but the place of impact was not on the ground, of the third -- that is fourth one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to these three shells that you investigated, did you have any information that there were any casualties in respect of this incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the investigating magistrate was told that children who were playing with their sleds had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that investigating magistrate is Zdenko Eterovic. From your report, you would be able to remember it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the report says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the method which you used to investigate these three impact sites, was that the same or a different method from which you used to investigate other incidents?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Completely the same or completely --

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- identical. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Identical, identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in respect to the site in front of number 3 Cetinska Street, was it your finding that the shell came from the direction of the west?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said that is the direction of the Institute of the Blind?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the shell -- and I wish to take you very quickly through this. That impact point was on the asphalt traffic lane at 3 Cetinska Street?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You investigated a second shell which fell in front of number 4 Klare Zetkin Street?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was it your finding that it came from a west-northwest direction?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sorry, but I note that this is not an expert. This is a witness, and my impression is that there was a series of questions where proper names and place names and so on and so forth as given by these seem to me to be leading questions. And of course, Mr. President, I stand to be corrected if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have only asked him what is written here in the document which he has already indicated that he participated in preparing. I am quickly trying to get him to confirm parts of it, just for the record, so I can move on. I am not leading the witness into anything that is not before him already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a leading question; at the same time, it merely asked the witness to confirm whether it is correct what he stated in his report. So that extent, the question is admissible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I will be guided by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you confirm what is recorded in the report in respect to the shell at number 4 Klare Cetkin Street, that it fell on the curb between the traffic lane and the sidewalk?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I can -- I mean I confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in respect to these first -- or I shouldn't say "first." These two shells which you have spoken of, that which fell at 3 Cetinska Street on the asphalt traffic lane and that which fell at 4 Klara Cetkin Street --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really very sorry, but I wish to check certain things. Once again I don't know if you follow too closely, but if one look at 00268180, then this is completely legible, and possible there are some interpretation -- translation problems. Of course, the Defence can perfectly read Serbian, but we wonder if there was some translation problem. The Defence also has a copy which might be more legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we experienced yesterday that although it has not been established yet that perhaps because of the bad copies, subsequently translation suffered from that as well. Do you have any better available copy of especially I would say 0026-8182.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have to make an effort to find a better copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Stamp, I noticed several times now that bad copies are produced where better copies could have been available. It looks as if while copying, no one looks at the result, which is not what we expect someone who copies documents does. I think the Defence is not in a position to check the -- whether there's a correct translation of this, and we do not know whether this translation has been produced on the basis of these bad copies or on better copies. So what do you intend to do about it? It's not acceptable as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We will make efforts to have the best possible copies for the Defence for tomorrow. I don't think I'll be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can't imagine that you'll be able to use the three minutes. Can you use the three minutes' time for other purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I shall do so. But may I say something which I said I think it was Friday or Monday. If there's a part of a document which we give to the Defence which they have a problem with, we are available, and we could proceed much more quickly. I say so because we are under huge pressures now with these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you indicate to us whether when you were with -- for the first time with a copy of Exhibit P2171 whether it was as badly legible as this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I don't really know when. I can check that. But what I'm trying to say that on several occasions or at least on one occasion I interceded with the Prosecution saying be careful because this system does not work because your copy -- copies of poor quality. We talked to technicians and explained that to the Prosecution, and the answer was that it wasn't the time. And I am -- and I will satisfy myself with this, but we simply cannot work like this. We simply cannot work like this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what I'm trying to find out is that since you know that this document would be used in Court, and you have good reasons to complain about the quality, whether you could have done it prior to the presentation of this document in Court. I mean as you might have noticed, I blame the Prosecution for producing a bad copy if there's a better one available. If this bad copy would have been given to you prior to this Court hearing, I blame you for not asking for a better copy. And so I would say I would blame both parties, then, for losing time in Court, the one by producing bad copies; the other one by not indicating it at an earlier stage. Well, Mr. Stamp, I don't think it's of any use to start a new subject for just one minute and a half. It's not the first time that we are confronted with this problem. So would you please at the beginning -- I mean, the Chamber can't see it because we're only confronted with these documents at the very moment of tendering them and presenting them to the witness. But everyone else could have seen it or could have asked for a better copy once they noticed it. We've got one minute left. Is there anything you'd like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to emphasise that we are prepared to facilitate Defence as much as possible. All we need to do is to be told. The Defence got this document in 2000, another copy in November 2001, and about a month ago, they were informed that we would be seeking to introduce this document through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that all that has to be done first of all is that good copies are made, and second that you're informed if the quality of the copies is not satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it comes down to both parties at this moment as far as I can see. Yes, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I repeat this: I generally said at the very beginning of this case, I indicated at the very beginning, that the copies simply do not allow us to work properly. It's really too much work in view of the 41.000 documents that we received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once you know that a document will be used, if it's not legible, I expect you to raise the issue prior to the hearing with the Prosecution and not come up with it at the very moment when presented. Mr. Sabljica, we will resume your examination by the parties tomorrow. When I say 9.00 this time, I really intend it to be 9.00. Once again apologies that you had to wait for such a long time. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, same courtroom, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
